content.overview: The public-trust doctrine holds that the State is the trustee of certain natural resources — such as air, water, forests and ecological commons — for the benefit of the public. The State cannot abdicate that fiduciary obligation by permitting private appropriation that destroys the trust resource. M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath applied the doctrine in the Indian environmental context.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Natural resource held for the public? (2) State as trustee? (3) Private use destroying the trust? (4) Distinguish from polluter pays?
content.study:
Public trust is about ownership and stewardship of commons, not primarily about who pays for pollution (polluter pays) or when to regulate under uncertainty (precaution).

Case already in migrated file (retained): M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997) 1 SCC 388. No new case invented.

sections.heading: State as trustee
sections.body: The State holds natural resources in trust for the public and cannot treat them as disposable private property of the government.

sections.heading: Protected resources
sections.body: Typically air, water, rivers, forests and ecological commons of public importance.

sections.heading: Fiduciary limit
sections.body: Private use or grant that destroys or permanently appropriates the trust resource is inconsistent with the doctrine.

sections.heading: Kamal Nath
sections.body: Public-trust doctrine applied to environmental protection of a river and ecological resources.

sections.heading: Remedies
sections.body: Directions restoring the trust resource, restraining destructive private use, and related environmental relief.

examples.title: River diversion for private project
examples.body: A private project permanently damages a river stretch held for public ecological use — public-trust analysis supports restraint and restoration.

hypotheticals.question: May the State lease a critical ecological commons for private destruction without public-trust scrutiny?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Under the public-trust doctrine the State holds such resources for the public and cannot abdicate that fiduciary duty.

rows.right: Cost allocation after or during harm.

misconceptions.trap: Public trust means no private use of any natural resource is ever allowed.
misconceptions.correction: The doctrine restrains destruction or abdication of the trust; regulated compatible use is a separate question.
